q: Kwashiorkor manifestations include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: A high-calorie diet as the cause
e: SAM with oedema (kwashiorkor) is mainly protein deficiency with infection, not a high-calorie diet; apathy, hair changes, hypotonia and depigmentation are features.

q: All are true in kwashiorkor EXCEPT:
o: It is defined as a body weight below 60% of expected
e: A weight below 60% of expected without oedema is SAM without oedema (marasmus); in SAM with oedema the weight may be near normal because the oedema hides the loss.

q: The following statements are true regarding kwashiorkor EXCEPT:
o: Oedema is essential for the diagnosis
Hepatomegaly is due to fatty infiltration
e: Adaptation to starvation (using fat and muscle stores) is SAM without oedema (marasmus); SAM with oedema is a failure of adaptation.

q: The most characteristic laboratory finding in kwashiorkor is:
e: Low serum albumin is the most characteristic change in SAM with oedema and contributes to the oedema.

q: In kwashiorkor, all the following are true EXCEPT:
o: Usually occurs after weaning, at 1–3 years
e: SAM with oedema (kwashiorkor) is mainly protein deficiency; total energy deficiency causes SAM without oedema (marasmus).

q: An 18-month-old has MUAC 12.8 cm and bilateral pitting oedema of both feet. What is the classification?
e: Bilateral pitting oedema means SAM whatever the weight or MUAC.

q: A 2-year-old with SAM is alert, has oedema of both feet only, no medical complication and eats the RUTF test amount. Best management?
o: Outpatient therapeutic programme with RUTF at home
Nutrition counselling and review in 3 months
e: Uncomplicated SAM that passes the appetite test is treated in OTP with RUTF and weekly visits.

q: Which child with SAM can be treated as an outpatient?
o: A 2-year-old with oedema of the face and whole body
A 3-year-old who refuses RUTF at the appetite test
A 20-month-old, alert, oedema of the feet, passes the appetite test
e: An infant under 6 months who is not feeding well, oedema +++, a failed appetite test and medical complications all need admission.

q: The rehydration fluid of choice for a child with SAM and watery diarrhoea without shock is:
e: ReSoMal has less sodium and more potassium (Na 45, K 40 mmol/L) than ORS; IV fluid is only for shock.

q: The only indication for IV fluids in a child with SAM is:
e: Shock: 15 ml/kg over 1 hour; all other dehydration is treated slowly with ReSoMal.

q: A child with SAM has blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L and is conscious. Best next step?
o: 50 ml of 10% glucose orally or by NGT, then F-75
Wait for the next feed in 3 hours
e: Conscious: 50 ml of 10% glucose orally or by NGT; IV 10% glucose 5 ml/kg is for the unconscious child.

q: Iron supplementation in SAM should be:
o: Given IV in the first week
Started in the rehabilitation phase when the child gains weight
e: Iron is not given in the stabilisation phase because it worsens infection; start in rehabilitation (week 2).

q: On day 1 of inpatient treatment of SAM the child should receive:
e: Stabilisation starts with F-75 (75 kcal/100 ml) 11 ml/kg 2-hourly day and night.

q: The commonest cause of death in children with SAM is:
e: Infection (bronchopneumonia, sepsis) often has no fever in SAM, so every child gets antibiotics.

q: During transition to F-100, the pulse rises by 25/min and the breathing by 5/min. Best next step?
e: These are early signs of heart failure from feeding too fast: reduce the volume, then increase slowly.

q: The main advantage of RUTF for home treatment of SAM is that it:
o: Needs no water or cooking, so it is not contaminated
Is only for infants under 6 months
e: RUTF is a ready-to-eat paste (500 kcal per sachet) that needs no water, so it is safe at home.

q: A child is cured of SAM when:
o: The oedema has gone for 2 days
MUAC ≥ 12.5 cm (or WFH ≥ −2 SD) with no oedema on 2 consecutive visits
The appetite test is passed once
Serum albumin is normal on day 3
e: Cure (WHO 2023): the admission criterion is normal and there is no oedema, on 2 consecutive visits.

q: Hair with alternating bands of pale and dark colour in a malnourished child is called:
e: The flag sign records periods of poor and better nutrition (kwashiorkor).
